question: A 52-year-old woman presents with severe unilateral facial pain in the distribution of the right mandibular (V3) and maxillary (V2) branches of the trigeminal nerve, triggered by chewing, talking and touching the face. The pain is electric shock-like lasting seconds. She also has right shoulder pain. Per NICE CKS, what is the diagnosis and first-line treatment?

options.B: Trigeminal neuralgia — carbamazepine 100mg twice daily, titrating up to 200-400mg twice daily; the most effective first-line treatment; monitor FBC and LFTs; if refractory: gabapentin, lamotrigine or referral for surgical/radiofrequency ablation

explanation.correct: Trigeminal neuralgia: the most severe pain known in medicine — paroxysmal electric shock-like pain in the distribution of one or more branches of the trigeminal nerve (V1, V2, V3 or combination). Triggered by light touch (chewing, talking, cold wind, face washing). Unilateral. Lasts seconds to 2 minutes. No neurological deficit. Per NICE CKS: first-line treatment is carbamazepine (sodium channel blocker) — start at 100mg twice daily, titrate to 200-400mg twice daily to symptom relief. Monitor: FBC (aplastic anaemia — rare), LFTs, sodium (hyponatraemia), check HLA-B*1502 in patients of Han Chinese/Asian descent before starting (risk of SJS/TEN). If bilateral or in patients under 50: MRI to exclude secondary causes (MS, vascular compression).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Atypical facial pain is persistent, less well-defined and less severely paroxysmal — tricyclics are used for neuropathic facial pain but carbamazepine is for trigeminal neuralgia.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Trigeminal neuralgia: electric shock paroxysmal facial pain. Carbamazepine first-line per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — TMJ disorder causes dull aching jaw pain aggravated by chewing — not electric shock-like severe paroxysmal pain.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Cluster headache causes periorbital/temporal pain with autonomic features — not facial nerve distribution pain.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Dental abscess causes localised dental pain with swelling — not this distribution and character.

question: A 35-year-old man was involved in a serious road traffic accident 8 months ago in which a child was killed (he was not at fault). He experiences intrusive flashbacks of the incident, nightmares, avoids driving, is emotionally numb and hypervigilant. He has survivor guilt and has not responded to watchful waiting. Per NICE NG116, what is the recommended treatment?

options.A: Long-term benzodiazepine for anxiety — first-line for PTSD
options.B: Trauma-focused psychological therapy: Eye Movement Desensitisation and Reprocessing (EMDR) or trauma-focused Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (tf-CBT) — both equally recommended by NICE NG116 as first-line for PTSD; should be offered to all adults with PTSD; EMDR involves bilateral eye movements while processing the traumatic memory
options.C: Sertraline only — SSRIs are first-line for all PTSD
options.D: Group therapy is preferred over individual therapy for all PTSD cases
options.E: Watchful waiting for 12 months before starting any treatment

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG116 (Post-traumatic stress disorder), trauma-focused psychological therapies are first-line for PTSD: (1) EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitisation and Reprocessing) — involves bilateral stimulation (eye movements, tapping) while the patient recalls the traumatic memory; disrupts reconsolidation of traumatic memories; recommended for PTSD across all age groups and trauma types per NICE NG116; (2) Trauma-focused CBT (tf-CBT) — includes exposure to traumatic memories (imaginal and in-vivo) and cognitive restructuring. Pharmacological treatment: SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) or venlafaxine — only if psychological therapy is declined, not available or insufficient; NOT first-line. Benzodiazepines: NOT recommended for PTSD (may worsen long-term outcomes by interfering with fear extinction). This patient's PTSD criteria are clearly met (>1 month duration, hyperarousal, re-experiencing, avoidance).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Benzodiazepines are specifically NOT recommended for PTSD treatment per NICE NG116.
explanation.B: CORRECT — EMDR or trauma-focused CBT are first-line for PTSD per NICE NG116.
explanation.C: Incorrect — SSRIs are second-line for PTSD (when psychological therapy is not available/declined) — not first-line.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Individual trauma-focused therapy is first-line — group therapy can be offered but is not the primary recommendation.
explanation.E: Incorrect — After 8 months of symptoms with significant impairment, watchful waiting is no longer appropriate — active treatment should start.

reference: NICE NG116 — Post-traumatic stress disorder. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng116

question: A 55-year-old woman has a stamping gait and becomes unsteady when she closes her eyes (positive Romberg test). She has loss of vibration and proprioception in both feet but motor power is normal. Per neuroanatomical principles, which structure is affected and what are the likely causes?

options.A: Cerebellum — causes ataxia that does not worsen on eye closure
options.B: Dorsal columns (posterior columns) of the spinal cord — carry vibration, proprioception and discriminative touch; loss causes sensory ataxia (stamping gait, positive Romberg — worse with eyes closed as visual compensation removed); causes: subacute combined degeneration of the cord (vitamin B12 deficiency), tabes dorsalis (neurosyphilis), MS, Friedreich's ataxia, compressive myelopathy
options.C: Anterior horn cells — cause lower motor neurone weakness
options.D: Spinothalamic tract — causes pain and temperature loss
options.E: Cerebral cortex — causes contralateral sensory and motor loss

explanation.correct: Dorsal column (posterior column) sensory ataxia: the dorsal columns carry: vibration (128 Hz tuning fork), proprioception (joint position sense) and discriminative touch/two-point discrimination. Dorsal column lesion → sensory ataxia: patient compensates for proprioceptive loss by using vision; remove vision (close eyes) → instability (positive Romberg = cannot stand eyes closed). Romberg is POSITIVE (sensory ataxia) vs cerebellar ataxia (positive finger-nose, dysdiadochokinesia, wide-based gait that does NOT worsen significantly on eye closure). Key causes: (1) Subacute combined degeneration — vitamin B12 deficiency (dorsal AND lateral columns); (2) Tabes dorsalis — neurosyphilis; (3) MS plaques affecting posterior columns; (4) Friedreich's ataxia; (5) Compressive myelopathy. Investigations: serum B12, syphilis serology, MRI spine.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Cerebellar ataxia causes incoordination that does NOT worsen on eye closure (Romberg negative) — dysdiadochokinesia, intention tremor, nystagmus.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Dorsal columns: vibration + proprioception loss + positive Romberg = sensory ataxia from posterior column lesion.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Anterior horn cell lesions cause LMN weakness (wasting, fasciculations) — not sensory ataxia.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature — spinothalamic lesion causes dissociated sensory loss (pain/temperature affected, vibration/proprioception spared).
explanation.E: Incorrect — Cortical lesions cause contralateral hemisensory loss and cortical sensory loss — not the bilateral dorsal column picture.

reference: Neuroanatomy — Dorsal column pathway. NICE CKS — Vitamin B12 deficiency. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/vitamin-b12-deficiency/

question: A 45-year-old man presents with severe unilateral periorbital pain occurring in clusters — attacks lasting 15-180 minutes, 1-8 times per day for 4 weeks at the same time each year, with ipsilateral lacrimation, nasal congestion and ptosis during attacks. Per NICE CG150 and NICE CKS, what is the first-line prophylactic treatment?

options.B: Verapamil 240-960mg daily — first-line prophylaxis for episodic and chronic cluster headache; requires ECG before starting (PR interval monitoring) and during dose titration; lithium is second-line

explanation.correct: Cluster headache: a trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia — the most painful primary headache disorder. Features: strictly unilateral periorbital/temporal pain; ipsilateral autonomic features (lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, miosis, ptosis, conjunctival injection, facial sweating); attacks 15-180 minutes; 1-8 attacks/day; clusters lasting weeks to months. Per NICE CKS and British Association for the Study of Headache (BASH) guidelines: Acute treatment: 100% oxygen 12-15 L/min via non-rebreather mask (highly effective) + subcutaneous or nasal sumatriptan. Prophylaxis: verapamil 240mg TDS (first-line) — dose may need to be as high as 960mg/day; requires ECG monitoring for PR prolongation (AV block risk). ECG: before starting, after each dose increase, and every 6 months on maintenance. Second-line prophylaxis: lithium, topiramate, methysergide.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Propranolol is first-line prophylaxis for migraine — not cluster headache.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Verapamil is first-line prophylaxis for cluster headache per NICE CKS/BASH; ECG monitoring required.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Amitriptyline is first-line prophylaxis for chronic tension-type headache — not cluster headache.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Topiramate is a second-line option for cluster headache and migraine prevention — not first-line for cluster.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Sumatriptan is for acute attack treatment — daily sumatriptan is not appropriate and risks overuse headache.

reference: NICE CKS — Cluster headache. BASH — Cluster headache guidelines. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/cluster-headache/

question: A 65-year-old man was diagnosed with a tremor 20 years ago. The tremor is bilateral, affects both hands equally, is present with sustained posture (action/postural tremor) and improves with alcohol. There are no other neurological signs. He has been stable for 20 years. Per NICE CKS, what is the diagnosis and management?

options.B: Essential tremor — most common movement disorder; bilateral postural/kinetic tremor, often improving with alcohol, positive family history; management: propranolol (first-line) 40-120mg daily or primidone; refer to neurology only if diagnosis uncertain or disability is severe
options.C: Intention tremor from cerebellar disease — MRI brain

explanation.correct: Essential tremor (ET): the most common movement disorder, affecting 4-5% of people over 65. Features: bilateral (usually hands — may also affect head 'yes-yes' or 'no-no', voice), postural or kinetic tremor (present with sustained posture and movement — NOT at rest), frequency 6-12 Hz, improving with alcohol and worsening with stress/caffeine, positive family history (~50% autosomal dominant). No other neurological signs. Per NICE CKS: pharmacological treatment: propranolol (first-line) 40-120mg daily or primidone 50-750mg daily. If refractory: referral to neurology for consideration of botulinum toxin, deep brain stimulation (severe disabling ET). Parkinson's: resting tremor (4-6 Hz), unilateral onset, bradykinesia, rigidity, postural instability — distinct from ET.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Parkinson's tremor is RESTING (pill-rolling), unilateral onset, associated with bradykinesia and rigidity — not bilateral action tremor improving with alcohol.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Essential tremor: bilateral postural/kinetic, improves with alcohol, 20-year stable history. Propranolol first-line per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Cerebellar intention tremor worsens as the limb approaches a target (finger-nose test positive) and is associated with dysmetria/dysdiadochokinesia.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Wilson's disease presents in young adults (<40) with liver disease, Kayser-Fleischer rings and neuropsychiatric features — not a 65-year-old with 20-year stable tremor.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Drug-induced tremor is possible but 20 years of stable tremor without drug history change makes ET the diagnosis.

question: A 70-year-old woman presents with a 2-year history of gradually worsening unilateral (right) resting tremor, bradykinesia, and rigidity. She also has a shuffling gait and reduced arm swing on the right. Per NICE NG71, what is the diagnosis and first-line treatment?

options.B: Parkinson's disease — diagnosed clinically by presence of bradykinesia plus at least one of: rest tremor, rigidity; first-line treatment for motor symptoms: levodopa (combined with carbidopa/benserazide as co-careldopa/co-beneldopa) OR dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole); refer to Parkinson's disease specialist
options.C: Drug-induced parkinsonism — review medications for dopamine antagonists
options.E: Progressive supranuclear palsy — vertical gaze palsy

explanation.correct: Parkinson's disease: diagnosis is clinical per UK Parkinson's Disease Society Brain Bank criteria. Bradykinesia (slowness of movement — cardinal feature) PLUS at least one of: resting tremor (4-6 Hz, 'pill-rolling', disappears with voluntary movement), rigidity (lead-pipe or cogwheel), postural instability. Usually asymmetric onset. Other features: micrographia, hypomimia, hypophonia, shuffling gait, reduced arm swing. Per NICE NG71: refer to a Parkinson's disease specialist (neurologist or geriatrician with expertise); DaTSCAN if diagnostic uncertainty. First-line pharmacological treatment: levodopa (as co-careldopa) — most effective for motor symptoms; dopamine agonists (pramipexole) — fewer motor complications but more neuropsychiatric side effects. Choice depends on patient age, comorbidities and patient preference.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Essential tremor has bilateral postural/kinetic tremor without bradykinesia or rigidity — propranolol is not appropriate for Parkinson's.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Parkinson's disease: bradykinesia + rest tremor + rigidity. Levodopa or dopamine agonist first-line per NICE NG71.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Drug-induced parkinsonism is possible (dopamine antagonists: metoclopramide, antipsychotics, haloperidol) — but this 2-year progressive unilateral history without relevant drug history points to idiopathic PD.
explanation.D: Incorrect — MSA causes parkinsonism with prominent autonomic failure (orthostatic hypotension, urinary incontinence, impotence) early in the disease course.
explanation.E: Incorrect — PSP causes vertical gaze palsy (inability to look down), severe postural instability with early falls, and axial rigidity — distinct from typical PD.

reference: NICE NG71 — Parkinson's disease in adults. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71

question: A 35-year-old man wakes up with right-sided facial weakness. He cannot close his right eye, his right forehead is smooth (unable to wrinkle), and he has a drooping right corner of his mouth. Examination shows no other neurological abnormality and no vesicles. Per NICE CKS, what is the diagnosis and key clinical finding that distinguishes this from a central (UMN) facial palsy?

options.A: Central (UMN) facial palsy — MRI brain urgently required
options.B: Bell's palsy (lower motor neurone facial nerve palsy) — inability to wrinkle the forehead distinguishes LMN from UMN facial palsy; in UMN (stroke/tumour) the forehead is SPARED (bilateral cortical representation of forehead muscles); in LMN (Bell's palsy), the ENTIRE face including forehead is affected
options.C: Ramsay Hunt syndrome — vesicular rash in ear and facial palsy from HZV
options.D: Parotid tumour — slow onset facial weakness

explanation.correct: Bell's palsy: idiopathic lower motor neurone (LMN) facial nerve (CN VII) palsy, usually caused by HSV-1 reactivation in the facial canal. Key examination finding: involves the ENTIRE ipsilateral face INCLUDING the forehead (inability to raise eyebrow, wrinkle forehead, close eye). UMN facial palsy (central — stroke, tumour): forehead is SPARED because the forehead muscles receive bilateral cortical input from both hemispheres; only the lower face is affected on the contralateral side. Per NICE CKS: Bell's palsy treatment — oral prednisolone 50mg daily for 10 days (started within 72 hours — significantly improves recovery); eye protection (lubricating drops, taping at night — risk of corneal exposure injury); antiviral (aciclovir) — NICE CKS does not recommend routinely; consider if Ramsay Hunt suspected. Most recover fully by 3-6 months.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Forehead involvement confirms LMN (Bell's palsy) — not UMN. MRI is not urgently indicated for typical Bell's palsy.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Bell's palsy: LMN CN VII palsy — forehead affected. Key distinction from UMN (forehead spared). Prednisolone within 72 hours per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Ramsay Hunt syndrome has LMN facial palsy with vesicular rash in the ear canal/pinna (HZV reactivation) — no vesicles here.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Parotid tumours cause gradual onset facial weakness — not acute overnight onset.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Stroke causes UMN facial palsy (forehead spared) with contralateral limb weakness — this patient has forehead involvement confirming Bell's palsy.

question: A 38-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting MS has spasticity causing painful leg cramps and increased muscle tone. Per NICE NG220 and MS Society guidance, what is the first-line pharmacological treatment for MS-related spasticity?

options.A: Diazepam — benzodiazepine first-line for all spasticity
options.B: Baclofen (GABA-B receptor agonist) — first-line oral antispasticity agent for MS-related spasticity per NICE NG220; alternative: tizanidine; gabapentin also used; physiotherapy must accompany pharmacological treatment; Sativex (delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol + cannabidiol) is NICE-approved for MS spasticity not responsive to other treatments
options.D: IV methylprednisolone for all MS-related symptoms
options.E: Surgical rhizotomy — first-line for MS spasticity

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG220 (Multiple sclerosis in adults: management) and MS Society guidance, management of MS spasticity: Non-pharmacological: physiotherapy (stretching, positioning), hydrotherapy — essential alongside medication. First-line pharmacological: baclofen (GABA-B agonist) — start 5mg TDS, titrate to 20-30mg TDS; tizanidine (alpha-2 agonist) — alternative with similar efficacy; gabapentin — especially if neuropathic pain component. Sativex (nabiximols — oromucosal cannabis spray): NICE-approved (TA 633, 2019) for moderate-severe MS spasticity not adequately controlled by other antispastics; intrathecal baclofen pump for severe refractory spasticity. Benzodiazepines (diazepam): occasionally used but cause significant sedation and dependence — not preferred. IV methylprednisolone is for MS relapses (reduces duration) — not for symptom management.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Diazepam causes significant sedation and dependence — baclofen is preferred first-line for MS spasticity.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Baclofen first-line for MS spasticity + physiotherapy per NICE NG220. Sativex for refractory cases.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Prednisolone is not used for spasticity management — it is used for acute MS relapses.
explanation.D: Incorrect — IV methylprednisolone shortens MS relapse duration — it does not treat chronic spasticity.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Surgical procedures are last resort for severe refractory spasticity — not first-line.

reference: NICE NG220 — Multiple sclerosis in adults. NICE TA633 — Sativex. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng220

question: A 72-year-old man presents to his GP with a 30-minute episode of sudden painless complete loss of vision in his left eye, like 'a curtain coming down', which resolved completely. He has hypertension and smokes. Per NICE NG128, what is the diagnosis and immediate management?

options.B: Amaurosis fugax (transient monocular vision loss) — a TIA equivalent from the retinal circulation; requires same-day specialist TIA assessment (within 24 hours per NICE NG128); dual antiplatelet (aspirin 300mg stat + clopidogrel); carotid Doppler USS and cardiac monitoring urgently — risk of stroke is highest in first 48-72 hours
options.E: Reassure — transient vision loss in elderly is benign

explanation.correct: Amaurosis fugax (retinal TIA/transient monocular blindness): transient (minutes to hours), complete or partial, painless monocular visual loss — caused by emboli (from carotid artery atheroma or cardiac source) to the central retinal artery or its branches. Resolves completely — distinguishes from permanent visual loss. Per NICE NG128 (Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s): amaurosis fugax is classified as a TIA and managed as such. SAME-DAY specialist assessment (within 24 hours for TIA): aspirin 300mg stat (if not contraindicated), rapid brain imaging (DW-MRI), carotid Doppler USS (if carotid territory TIA), cardiac monitoring (AF detection), echocardiogram, bloods (FBC, glucose, lipids, HbA1c). Secondary prevention: dual antiplatelet (aspirin + clopidogrel) for 21 days then single antiplatelet; statin; antihypertensive. Carotid endarterectomy if significant carotid stenosis (>50%).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Migraine visual aura typically involves both eyes (cortical spreading depression), is gradual (march), and often positive phenomena (zigzag lines) — not sudden complete monocular curtain.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Amaurosis fugax = retinal TIA. Same-day TIA clinic + aspirin 300mg + carotid Doppler per NICE NG128.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Retinal detachment causes a shadow from the periphery with preceding floaters/flashes and does NOT resolve completely within 30 minutes.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Optic neuritis causes sub-acute visual loss over days with pain on eye movement — not sudden transient monocular blindness.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Transient monocular vision loss has the same stroke risk as a hemispheric TIA — same-day assessment is mandatory.

reference: NICE NG128 — Stroke and TIA. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng128

question: A 62-year-old man presents with a vesicular rash in the right ear canal and right concha, combined with right-sided lower motor neurone facial palsy and right-sided ear pain. He also has reduced hearing in the right ear. Per NICE CKS, what is the diagnosis and treatment?

options.B: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus) — varicella zoster virus reactivation in the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve; oral aciclovir 800mg five times daily for 7 days PLUS oral prednisolone 60mg daily for 7 days (combination therapy); eye protection for corneal exposure

explanation.correct: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus): HZV reactivation in the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve. Triad: (1) Vesicular rash in the ear (pinna, external auditory canal — HZV dermatomal rash in CN VII/VIII territory); (2) Ipsilateral LMN facial palsy; (3) Otalgia (often severe). May also cause: sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo (if HZV affects CN VIII — cochlear/vestibular branches). Per NICE CKS: combination treatment within 72 hours: aciclovir 800mg five times daily for 7 days + prednisolone 60mg daily for 7 days. Better facial nerve recovery with combination therapy than with either alone. Eye protection mandatory (risk of corneal exposure injury from incomplete eye closure). Prognosis for facial nerve recovery is worse than Bell's palsy (~50-70% complete recovery vs >90% in Bell's).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Bell's palsy has no vesicular rash — it is treated with prednisolone alone (antivirals not routinely recommended by NICE for Bell's). Ramsay Hunt requires combination antiviral + steroid.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Ramsay Hunt: HZV in geniculate ganglion. Vesicular ear rash + facial palsy + ear pain. Aciclovir + prednisolone within 72 hours per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Otitis externa affects the ear canal with tragus tenderness but no facial nerve palsy or vesicular rash.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Malignant OE is Pseudomonas osteomyelitis of the skull base — affects immunocompromised/diabetic patients without vesicular rash.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Primary varicella causes widespread vesicular rash — not a localised ear rash with facial palsy in a 62-year-old.
